transcript.text: Bosch WTN85201GB condenser dryer not drying properly anymore, clothes still damp after 2 hrs. any ideas

The most common reason is restricted airflow: a fluff-loaded filter or blocked condenser makes a condenser dryer take far longer, and it can eventually reduce or cut the heat for protection. Less commonly it is a weak heater/thermal cut-out, or laundry going in too wet/too large a load. 1. With the dryer switched off and unplugged, clean the door fluff filter thoroughly. Remove all fluff from the mesh and the filter housing; a film from detergent/softener can also restrict it, so rinse and dry the filter if needed. 2. Open the lower front flap and clean the condenser/heat-exchanger area or lower filter, as applicable. Remove loose fluff carefully and rinse any removable condenser/filter only if the instructions permit it; let it drip-dry before refitting. A blockage here strongly supports an airflow cause. 3. Try a normal Cotton/extra-dry programme with a modest, well-spun load—roughly no more than two-thirds of the drum. Avoid a cool-air, refresh or very low-heat setting for this test. If the washing is coming out of the washer unusually wet, improve the washer spin first. 4. After 10–15 minutes, carefully check whether the drum and exhaust air feel noticeably warm. If it is warm but still takes ages after the cleaning, airflow, loading or drying-sensor issues remain most likely. If it is still cool, a heater or thermal safety fault becomes more likely and is an engineer repair after the airflow checks. If cleaning restores normal drying, no parts should be needed. Do not dismantle panels or test internal electrical parts yourself.
ok, will give those a go. door filter has fluff and a waxy film, rinsed it and water barely passes through until I scrubbed it. which one is the condenser, the bottom front flap?

On versions of this type it may reveal either a removable lower filter/cassette or the heat exchanger itself. With the dryer switched off and unplugged, open the flap and check for loose fluff. If there is a removable filter or cassette, take it out and clean it as the instructions allow, then let it drain before refitting. If you can only see fixed metal fins, gently vacuum or brush loose fluff from the accessible surface; do not poke the fins or force water into it. The waxy door filter is a very strong lead: that coating can restrict airflow almost like a blockage, so it may well be the main reason drying time has increased. Once the lower area is clean too, run a normal full-heat programme with a modest, well-spun load and see whether drying returns to normal.

Opened the flap and took the condenser out. The front face was matted with lint, never cleaned it before. Rinsed it with the shower head and it came clean. Anything else I should clean while it's out?

Yes — with it out, clean any loose lint from the condenser compartment and the seals/edges where the condenser sits, using a vacuum with a soft brush or a dry cloth. Do not poke or bend any fins, and do not spray water into the machine itself. Let the condenser drain well before refitting it, make sure it seats fully and the flap closes properly. The door filter should also be completely dry before use. The heavily coated door filter plus the matted condenser are more than enough to explain the poor drying, so this is very likely the fix rather than a failed heater. To prevent a repeat, clean the door filter after every load and rinse the condenser periodically. Run a normal warm programme with a modest, well-spun load once everything is back together.
vacuumed the fluff out of the slot behind the condenser housing too. Refitting now and will run a test cycle.

Before you start, switch it off and unplug it. Make sure the condenser is fully seated, the seals are clean and it is allowed to drain before the test. For prevention, clean the door filter after every load and rinse the condenser periodically—more often if you use fabric conditioner or dry lots of towels/pet bedding. If it still is not drying properly after a normal, well-spun modest load, it would then be worth checking whether it is warming after 10–15 minutes; but the blockage found is a very convincing explanation. Is there anything else you need help with?
Test cycle done. Clothes dry in about 100 minutes and the container is nearly full now. Looks sorted, thanks.

That suggests it: the coated door filter and matted condenser were restricting airflow. Dry clothes in about 100 minutes and a nearly full container show it is now heating, condensing and pumping water normally. Clean the door filter after each load, and rinse the condenser periodically—especially if fabric conditioner is used or you dry towels/pet bedding. No parts or engineer are needed on the evidence so far.

candidates: Restricted airflow from lint filter or condenser/heat-exchanger blockage (high)
Laundry too wet, load too large, or unsuitable programme/dryness setting (medium)
